payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
The false-positive problem that made AI detectors indefensible has largely been solved, and the objection that matters survives it intact. A verdict of 100% AI does not mean every word was generated, and the same paragraph scores differently depending on what surrounds it.

The false positives got fixed

For two years the strongest case against AI detectors was that they punished the wrong people. Seven tools run over ninety-one TOEFL essays in 2023 produced an average false positive rate of 61.3%, and the seven agreed on only eighteen of the ninety-one. That argument is now out of date. Epoch AI tested Pangram against 495 human-written texts this July and found zero false positives. Pangram's own technical paper reports a 0.0041% false-positive rate on English, comparable false-positive rates across more than a hundred languages, and a single false positive across 24,586 samples of writing by people who are not fluent English speakers.

The penalty on non-native writers was real, it ruined people, and it appears to have been engineered out. Conceding that costs nothing, because it was never the part that mattered.

The score is not a property of the text

Pangram cuts a document into segments, judges each one, and reports the proportion flagged. A verdict of 100% AI does not mean every word was generated. It means every segment was probably generated. Max Spero, who co-founded the company, told Nature that a paragraph judged human on its own can flip to AI once it sits inside a larger segment, and described a separate problem the firm calls jitter, where small edits shift the score by a large amount.

Read that plainly. The same paragraph earns different verdicts depending on what surrounds it. Whatever the number is measuring, it is not a fixed attribute of the words being judged, which is a strange thing to put in front of a disciplinary panel.

Pangram shipped into Substack in July. Readers now see a verdict on posts while they read them.

The tool also goes quiet in the other direction. When Pangram tested consumer AI making substantial modifications to human-written student essays, its own model still called the results fully human 41% of the time. Mixed writing is where nearly everyone now lives, and it is the case the tools handle worst.

Nobody outside can check it, nobody inside can answer it

Nature reports that only the accuracy rates the firms announce from internal testing can be current, and that those are not externally verified. Tim Requarth, who studies science communication at NYU Langone Health, puts the structural version of it in one line: third-party evaluations will always trail whichever detector is current. GPTZero shipped twenty-three model updates in a single year. Any independent number is a measurement of a tool that no longer exists.

Then the cases. Elena Vicario, research integrity director at Frontiers, wrote a post that Pangram scored 100% AI, revised to 96% after the next model shipped. She says the draft and the ideas in it were entirely her own and that she used AI to polish the language. Two Nature news reports containing original interviews were also labelled 100% AI. Pangram and GPTZero disagreed with each other about which segments looked most machine-written. Both models are black boxes. Pangram's own technical report concedes the point, noting that its predictions are opaque and that the reasons behind any particular one are hard to account for.

So consider the position of the accused. The number is unexaminable, the thresholds are unpublished, the vendors disagree, and the tool that produced the verdict will be superseded before any appeal is heard. Nothing available returns a finding of human. A probabilistic accusation cannot be answered with more probability.

What the record does instead

Music runs the same experiment with the dispute arriving later and money attached to it. A takedown, a royalty split, a distributor deciding whether a delivery is what it claims to be. The score placed in front of that panel carries every property described above, and the fight over which vendor to believe is the fight the journals are already having, with a longer tail and no registrar at the end of it.

A writer holding a revision history is not arguing about a score. They have a different kind of object, one written while the work was happening, which no later model can recompute or revise. It resolves or it does not, and the same evidence stays good in ten years. Whether it is worth anything depends entirely on whether it existed before the dispute did. Almost nobody in music is making one.

payload.title: There is no test that returns human
